subject: DI02000021

intro_text.en: Unit 2 of Engineering Mathematics: the derivative as the slope of the tangent and as a limit, the standard derivatives, the sum, product and quotient rules, the chain rule, implicit and parametric curves, logarithmic differentiation, the second derivative, and the applications - velocity, acceleration and maxima or minima. Twenty-four fully solved numericals, each linked to a card.

h.en: 1.1 What a derivative is

body.en:
Definition

The derivative of y = f(x) at a point is the slope of the tangent to the curve there. It is obtained as the limit of the slope of a chord when one end of the chord slides towards the other:

dy/dx = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h

The three-step method

  1. Write f(x + h) and subtract f(x).
  2. Divide the difference by h and simplify until the h cancels.
  3. Put h = 0 in the simplified expression.

Worked example

For f(x) = x²: [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h = (x² + 2xh + h² − x²)/h = 2x + h, and with h = 0 the answer is 2x. At x = 1 the slope is 2, which matches the tangent in the diagram.

Reading dy/dx

dy/dx is a single symbol for the derivative - not a fraction to be cancelled, and not dy divided by dx at the end of a question.

h.en: 1.2 First principles for roots and other awkward functions

body.en:
The rationalising trick

When f(x) contains a square root, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate first; the root disappears from the top and h cancels.

Worked example

For f(x) = √x: [√(x + h) − √x]/h, multiplied by [√(x + h) + √x]/[√(x + h) + √x], becomes h / {h[√(x + h) + √x]} = 1/[√(x + h) + √x]. With h = 0 this gives 1/(2√x).

When to use first principles

  • The syllabus asks for it directly, usually for x², x³, √x or 1/x.
  • It proves a standard result once; afterwards you may quote the table.
  • It is never the fastest route for a complicated function - use the rules.

Common mistake

Putting h = 0 too early. If h = 0 is substituted before the h in the denominator is cancelled, every question becomes 0/0 and no answer appears.

Using the table

For y = 3x² − 5x + 2 each term is differentiated separately: 6x − 5 + 0. At x = 2 the slope is 12 − 5 = 7.

Common mistake

Differentiating a constant to 1. The derivative of 2 is 0; only x (that is x¹) gives 1.

h.en: 1.4 Notation, and when a derivative does not exist

body.en:
Four ways to write the same thing

  • f′(x)
  • dy/dx
  • y′
  • D(f(x))

A derivative can fail to exist

At a sharp corner or a vertical tangent the two one-sided slopes disagree, so the limit of the chord slope has no single value. The function is then not differentiable at that point, even though it may be continuous there.

What the sign tells you

dy/dxThe curve is
positiverising as x increases
negativefalling as x increases
zeroflat - a stationary point (Unit 2.8)
Is every continuous function differentiable?

No. Continuity is necessary but not sufficient: a corner such as y = |x| at x = 0 is continuous yet has no derivative there.

title.en: 2. Working Rules: Sum, Product and Division

h.en: 2.1 Sum and difference

body.en:
Rule

(u ± v)′ = u′ ± v′ - differentiate term by term, keeping the signs.

Worked example

y = x³ + 2x² − 7x + 1 gives dy/dx = 3x² + 4x − 7. The constant 1 disappears.

With other functions

y = sin x + cos x gives cos x − sin x; y = 3eˣ − 2 log x gives 3eˣ − 2/x.

Common mistake

Applying the product rule to a sum. The product rule is for u times v, not u plus v.

h.en: 2.2 The product rule

body.en:
Rule

(uv)′ = u′v + uv′ - differentiate the first and keep the second, then keep the first and differentiate the second, and add.

Worked example

y = x²(3x + 5): u = x², v = 3x + 5, so dy/dx = 2x(3x + 5) + x²(3) = 6x² + 10x + 3x² = 9x² + 10x.

Second example

y = (x + 1)(x² + 3) gives 1·(x² + 3) + (x + 1)(2x) = 3x² + 2x + 3.

Common mistake

Writing (uv)′ = u′v′. For the example above that would give 2x·3 = 6x instead of 9x² + 10x.

Can you expand first instead?

Yes, when the bracket is easy: x²(3x + 5) = 3x³ + 5x² differentiates to 9x² + 10x as well. Use whichever is quicker, but the product rule is compulsory when the factors are trig, log or exponential.

h.en: 2.3 The quotient rule

body.en:
Rule

(u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′) / v² - note the minus sign and the order: the derivative of the top comes first.

Worked example

y = (2x + 1)/(x − 1): u = 2x + 1, v = x − 1, u′ = 2, v′ = 1. Then dy/dx = [2(x − 1) − (2x + 1)(1)]/(x − 1)² = (2x − 2 − 2x − 1)/(x − 1)² = −3/(x − 1)².

Second example

y = x/(x² + 1) gives [(1)(x² + 1) − x(2x)]/(x² + 1)² = (1 − x²)/(x² + 1)².

Common mistake

Swapping u and v, which flips the sign of the whole answer. Write u above v before you start, and keep the v² denominator until the last line.

h.en: 2.4 Choosing the rule before you differentiate

body.en:
A five-second check

The expression isUse
a sum of termsterm by term
a product of two functionsproduct rule
one function over anotherquotient rule
a function of a bracket, root or powerchain rule (next section)
x both in the base and in the powerlogarithmic differentiation

Order of work

  1. Name u and v (or u inside the bracket) on paper.
  2. Write the rule with u′ and v′ in place before substituting anything.
  3. Simplify only at the end, and cancel common factors.

Why the naming helps

Most lost marks in this unit are not wrong rules but wrong substitutions: u and v swapped, a missing minus, or a factor dropped in the middle line.

h.en: 3.1 A function of a function

body.en:
Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx - differentiate the outside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

Worked example

y = (3x + 2)⁵ with u = 3x + 2: dy/du = 5u⁴ and du/dx = 3, so dy/dx = 5u⁴ × 3 = 15(3x + 2)⁴.

The quick version

For y = [f(x)]ⁿ, dy/dx = n[f(x)]ⁿ⁻¹ × f′(x). For y = (2x − 1)⁷ that gives 7(2x − 1)⁶ × 2 = 14(2x − 1)⁶.

Common mistake

Forgetting the inside derivative. (3x + 2)⁵ differentiates to 5(3x + 2)⁴ only if the inside were x; with 3x + 2 the factor 3 is compulsory.

h.en: 3.2 Chain rule with trigonometric and exponential functions

body.en:
Patterns

  • y = sin(5x) → 5 cos(5x)
  • y = cos(3x) → −3 sin(3x)
  • y = e^(3x) → 3e^(3x)
  • y = e^(x²) → 2x e^(x²)

Worked examples

y = sin 5x: the outside is sin and the inside is 5x, so dy/dx = cos(5x) × 5 = 5 cos 5x.

y = e^(3x): the derivative of e^u is e^u, so dy/dx = e^(3x) × 3 = 3e^(3x).

Common mistake

Writing 5 cos x (inside untouched) or cos 5x (factor lost). Both parts must appear: the outer derivative evaluated at the inside, times the inside derivative.

h.en: 3.3 Chain rule with roots and logarithms

body.en:
Roots are powers

Write √(x² + 1) as (x² + 1)^(1/2); then dy/dx = (1/2)(x² + 1)^(−1/2) × 2x = x/√(x² + 1).

Logarithms

For y = log[f(x)], dy/dx = f′(x)/f(x). So y = log(sin x) gives cos x / sin x = cot x.

Deeper nesting

With three layers, multiply three factors. y = sin²(3x) is [sin 3x]², so dy/dx = 2 sin 3x × cos 3x × 3 = 6 sin 3x cos 3x.

Common mistake

Cancelling the root too early. Keep the fractional power until the last line, then convert back to a root form if the answer looks tidier.

h.en: 3.4 A checklist for any chain-rule question

body.en:
Four questions, in order

  1. What is the outermost operation? (power, sin, log, e)
  2. What is the whole inside expression? Call it u.
  3. What is du/dx?
  4. Multiply and then put u back in terms of x.

Speed check

y = (5x − 1)⁴ → 20(5x − 1)³; y = √(3x + 4) → 3/(2√(3x + 4)); y = log(2x + 5) → 2/(2x + 5).

Where it is used later

Every implicit, parametric and logarithmic derivative in this unit ends with a chain rule. Get this section solid and the next four become bookkeeping.

h.en: 4.1 When y is not given as a formula

body.en:
Definition

An implicit function is one where x and y are mixed in a single equation, such as x² + y² = 25. y is still a function of x, but it is not isolated.

Method

  1. Differentiate every term with respect to x.
  2. Every time you differentiate a y-term, multiply by dy/dx (chain rule).
  3. Collect the dy/dx terms on one side and factorise.
  4. Divide to finish.

Worked example

x² + y² = 25 gives 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y. At the point (3, 4) the slope is −3/4.

Why the minus appears

The dy/dx term arrives with a plus sign; moving it to the other side makes the answer negative - the standard shape for a circle.

h.en: 4.2 Products and squares inside an implicit equation

body.en:
Worked example

x² + xy + y² = 7. The middle term is a product, so it takes the product rule: 1·y + x·(dy/dx).

Differentiating: 2x + y + x(dy/dx) + 2y(dy/dx) = 0.

Factorising: (x + 2y)(dy/dx) = −(2x + y), so dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y).

A useful check

The formula is symmetric in x and y except for the swap, which is what you expect from a symmetric equation. Symmetry checks catch sign errors.

Common mistake

Writing the derivative of y² as 2y. It is 2y(dy/dx) - the chain rule never switches off for a y-term.

h.en: 4.3 Using an implicit derivative

body.en:
Slope and tangent at a point

Differentiate, then substitute the coordinates. For x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4) the slope is −3/4, so the tangent is y − 4 = (−3/4)(x − 3), that is 3x + 4y = 25.

Vertical tangents

Where the denominator of dy/dx becomes zero the slope is infinite: the tangent is vertical. On 2y = 0, that is at (5, 0) and (−5, 0) for the circle.

Why implicit differentiation is needed

Many engineering curves - a circle, an ellipse, a level curve of a graph - are given in implicit form. Isolating y would need two branches, and the slope formula would need a case split.

h.en: 5.1 x and y given separately in terms of t

body.en:
Rule

When x = f(t) and y = g(t), dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt).

Worked example

x = at², y = 2at: dx/dt = 2at and dy/dt = 2a, so dy/dx = 2a/(2at) = 1/t.

Why it works

Both x and y depend on t, so the slope is the rate of y per unit of t divided by the rate of x per unit of t. The chain rule in the form dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) says exactly that.

Common mistake

Inverting the ratio. dy/dx is dy/dt over dx/dt, not the other way round; the wrong way gives 2at/2a = t instead of 1/t.

h.en: 5.2 Parametric circles and ellipses

body.en:
Worked example

x = a cos θ, y = a sin θ (a circle of radius a): dx/dθ = −a sin θ and dy/dθ = a cos θ, so dy/dx = a cos θ / (−a sin θ) = −cot θ.

Checking against the implicit form

The same circle is x² + y² = a², whose implicit slope is −x/y = −a cos θ / a sin θ = −cot θ. Both methods agree - a good self-check in an exam.

Ellipse

For x = a cos θ, y = b sin θ the slope is −(b/a) cot θ, so the ellipse is flatter than the circle in the y-direction.

Common mistake

Differentiating sin θ to −cos θ. The derivative of sin is +cos; only cos gives −sin.

h.en: 5.3 Slopes, tangents and the value of the parameter

body.en:
Finding the point first

A parametric question usually gives the value of t or θ. Substitute that value into x and y to get the point, and into dy/dx to get the slope.

Example

x = t², y = 2t at t = 3: the point is (9, 6) and dy/dx = 1/t = 1/3, so the tangent is 3y = x − 9 + 18, that is x − 3y + 9 = 0.

What the parameter means

In kinematics t is time, so the parametric curve is the path of a particle and dy/dx is the direction of motion. In geometry t or θ is simply a label that runs along the curve.

Do you need d²y/dx² here?

The syllabus asks only for dy/dx of parametric curves. If asked, differentiate dy/dx with respect to t and divide by dx/dt.

h.en: 6.1 When the power contains x

body.en:
The problem

xˣ is neither xⁿ (power fixed) nor aˣ (base fixed), so neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies. Take logarithms first and the product rule does the work.

Method

  1. Take log of both sides: log y = x log x.
  2. Differentiate both sides: (1/y)(dy/dx) = 1·log x + x·(1/x).
  3. Simplify the right side: 1 + log x.
  4. Multiply by y: dy/dx = xˣ(1 + log x).

Why it is allowed

Both sides are positive for x > 0, so the logarithm is defined, and the chain rule gives the (1/y)(dy/dx) factor on the left.

h.en: 6.2 Products, quotients and powers together

body.en:
The trick in general

For y = (1 + x)ˣ: log y = x log(1 + x), so (1/y)(dy/dx) = log(1 + x) + x/(1 + x), giving dy/dx = (1 + x)ˣ[log(1 + x) + x/(1 + x)].

Also useful for long products and quotients

For y = x²(x + 1)³/(x − 2)⁴ the product and quotient rules give a very long expression. Taking logs turns it into a sum of three simple derivatives:

(1/y)(dy/dx) = 2/x + 3/(x + 1) − 4/(x − 2), then multiply by y.

Common mistake

Writing log(xˣ) = x log x and then forgetting to finish - the answer must be multiplied by y, not left as 1 + log x.

h.en: 6.3 Deciding to take the logarithm

body.en:
Take logs when

  • the variable appears in the exponent (xˣ, (sin x)ˣ, x^(1/x));
  • the expression is a long product or quotient that would need several rule applications;
  • an engineering formula is given as a product of powers, such as y = A x^n e^(−kx).

Do not take logs when

The base is a constant: aˣ differentiates straight to aˣ log a, and eˣ to eˣ. Logarithms there add work and a stray factor.

Worked mini-example

y = x^(1/x): log y = (1/x) log x = log x / x, so (1/y)(dy/dx) = (1 − log x)/x², giving dy/dx = x^(1/x)(1 − log x)/x².

The maximum of x^(1/x) is at x = e, which is exactly where that derivative vanishes - a neat link to the next section.

h.en: 7.1 The second derivative

body.en:
Definition

Differentiating dy/dx gives the second derivative d²y/dx², written y″ or f″(x). The syllabus asks for the second order; higher orders follow the same idea.

Worked examples

y = x⁴: y′ = 4x³ and y″ = 12x².

y = sin 3x: y′ = 3 cos 3x and y″ = −9 sin 3x - each differentiation multiplies by 3 and shifts the function.

What the second derivative means

y″The graph is
positivecurving upwards (concave up)
negativecurving downwards (concave down)
zeropossibly a point of inflexion - check the sign change

Notation trap

d²y/dx² is not (dy/dx)². The first is a second derivative; the second is the square of the first.

h.en: 7.2 Velocity and acceleration

body.en:
Kinematics from calculus

If s(t) is the position, then v = ds/dt and a = dv/dt = d²s/dt².

Worked example

s = t³ − 6t² + 8t − 4 gives v = 3t² − 12t + 8 and a = 6t − 12. At t = 3: v = 27 − 36 + 8 = −1 and a = 18 − 12 = 6.

Reading the signs

  • v > 0: moving in the positive direction; v < 0: moving backwards.
  • v = 0: momentarily at rest - a turning point of the motion.
  • a > 0 with v > 0: speeding up; a < 0 with v > 0: slowing down.

Units

If s is in metres and t in seconds, v is m/s and a is m/s². Keep the units in the final line; examiners give a mark for them.

h.en: 7.3 Maxima and minima: the method

body.en:
Steps

  1. Find f′(x).
  2. Solve f′(x) = 0 for the stationary points.
  3. Find f″(x) and evaluate it at each stationary point.
  4. f″ < 0 gives a maximum, f″ > 0 gives a minimum, f″ = 0 needs the first-derivative sign test.
  5. Substitute back into f(x) for the maximum or minimum value.

Worked example

f(x) = x³ − 3x + 2: f′ = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = 1 and x = −1; f″ = 6x, so f″(−1) = −6 (maximum, value 4) and f″(1) = 6 (minimum, value 0).

Common mistake

Answering with the x-value only. A maximum/minimum question normally asks for both the point and the value of the function there.

h.en: 7.4 A second maxima and minima example

body.en:
Worked example

f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x: f′ = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2), so the stationary points are x = 1 and x = 2.

f″ = 12x − 18 gives f″(1) = −6 (maximum, value 5) and f″(2) = 6 (minimum, value 4).

Word problems

For a rectangle of perimeter 20 cm, let the length be x; then the width is 10 − x and the area A = x(10 − x) = 10x − x². A′ = 10 − 2x = 0 gives x = 5, and A″ = −2 < 0 confirms a maximum of 25 cm² - a square.

Reading the answer back

Always say what the numbers mean in the words of the question (cm, cm², seconds, rupees). The calculus gives the turning point; the sentence gives the mark.

h.en: 7.5 Exam routine for a differentiation question

body.en:
Six lines that earn marks

  1. Write the function and name the rule you will use.
  2. Show u, v (or u inside) explicitly.
  3. Write the rule with u′, v′ before substituting.
  4. Simplify once, carefully.
  5. For applications, state f′(x) = 0 and solve.
  6. Finish with the second derivative, the sign test and a sentence.

Time saving

Standard derivatives (sin, cos, eˣ, log, xⁿ) should be quoted, not re-derived. First principles is only used when the question says so.

Accuracy habits

Keep brackets around negative terms until the last line, and never cancel across a plus sign. Most marks lost in this unit are sign and bracket slips, not method.

h.en: Practice 1. Differentiate f(x) = x² from first principles.

body.en:
Step 1: f(x + h) − f(x) = (x + h)² − x² = x² + 2xh + h² − x² = 2xh + h².

Step 2: divide by h, allowed because h ≠ 0, giving 2x + h.

Step 3: let h → 0, so f′(x) = 2x.

At x = 2 the slope is 4 and at x = −1 it is −2: the tangent falls left of the origin and rises to the right.

h.en: Practice 2. Differentiate √x from first principles.

body.en:
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate √(x + h) + √x.

The numerator becomes h, so the expression is 1/[√(x + h) + √x], and with h → 0 the derivative is 1/(2√x). At x = 4 the slope is 1/4.

h.en: Practice 3. Differentiate y = 4x³ − 6x² + 2x − 5 and find the slope at x = 1.

body.en:
Differentiate term by term: 12x² − 12x + 2.

At x = 1 the slope is 12 − 12 + 2 = 2. The constant −5 disappears because the derivative of a constant is zero.

h.en: Practice 4. Differentiate y = x²(2x − 3) by the product rule.

body.en:
u = x², v = 2x − 3, so u′ = 2x and v′ = 2.

(uv)′ = 2x(2x − 3) + x²(2) = 4x² − 6x + 2x² = 6x² − 6x.

Check by expanding: y = 2x³ − 3x² differentiates to 6x² − 6x.

h.en: Practice 5. Differentiate y = (3x + 1)/(x + 2) by the quotient rule.

body.en:
u = 3x + 1, v = x + 2, so u′ = 3 and v′ = 1.

dy/dx = [3(x + 2) − (3x + 1)]/(x + 2)² = (3x + 6 − 3x − 1)/(x + 2)² = 5/(x + 2)².

The answer is positive everywhere, so the curve always rises.

h.en: Practice 6. Differentiate y = (2x + 5)⁶.

body.en:
This is a function of a function, so use the chain rule with u = 2x + 5.

dy/dx = 6(2x + 5)⁵ × 2 = 12(2x + 5)⁵.

The factor 2 is compulsory; forgetting it is the most common error in this type.

h.en: Practice 7. Differentiate y = cos 4x and y = e^(5x).

body.en:
For y = cos 4x the inside is 4x, so dy/dx = −sin(4x) × 4 = −4 sin 4x.

For y = e^(5x) the derivative of e^u is e^u, so dy/dx = e^(5x) × 5 = 5e^(5x).

Notice that each derivative keeps the same function and only the inside factor changes.

h.en: Practice 8. Differentiate y = √(3x + 4).

body.en:
Write the root as a power, y = (3x + 4)^(1/2), and use the chain rule with u = 3x + 4.

dy/dx = (1/2)(3x + 4)^(−1/2) × 3, and the negative power puts the root underneath: dy/dx = 3/(2√(3x + 4)).

At x = 0 the slope is 3/(2√4) = 3/4, and the slope falls as x grows because the root in the denominator becomes larger.

h.en: Practice 9. Find dy/dx if x² + y² = 36, and the slope at (4, √20).

body.en:
Differentiate implicitly: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y.

At (4, √20) the slope is −4/√20 = −2/√5.

The tangent there is y − √20 = (−2/√5)(x − 4), which can be left in this form.

h.en: Practice 10. Find dy/dx if x² + 4xy + y² = 10.

body.en:
Differentiate term by term, using the product rule on 4xy: 2x + 4[y + x(dy/dx)] + 2y(dy/dx) = 0.

Collect the dy/dx terms: (4x + 2y)(dy/dx) = −(2x + 4y).

So dy/dx = −(x + 2y)/(2x + y) after dividing by 2.

h.en: Practice 11. Find dy/dx for x = 3t², y = 6t, and the slope at t = 2.

body.en:
dx/dt = 6t and dy/dt = 6, so dy/dx = 6/(6t) = 1/t.

At t = 2 the slope is 1/2, and the point is x = 12, y = 12.

The curve is a parabola and the slope falls as t grows, which matches the shape.

h.en: Practice 12. Find dy/dx for x = a sec θ, y = b tan θ.

body.en:
dx/dθ = a sec θ tan θ and dy/dθ = b sec²θ.

So dy/dx = b sec²θ /(a sec θ tan θ) = (b/a)(sec θ/tan θ) = (b/a) cosec θ.

Writing it as (b/a)·(1/sin θ) is the tidiest final form.

h.en: Practice 13. Differentiate y = xˣ by taking logarithms.

body.en:
Take logarithms: log y = x log x.

Differentiate: (1/y)(dy/dx) = log x + 1, so dy/dx = xˣ(1 + log x).

At x = 1 the slope is 1(0 + 1) = 1, and at x = 1/e it is zero, which is the minimum of the curve.

h.en: Practice 14. Find the second derivative of y = x⁵ + sin 2x.

body.en:
y′ = 5x⁴ + 2 cos 2x, using the chain rule on sin 2x.

Differentiate again: y″ = 20x³ − 4 sin 2x.

Each differentiation of sin 2x brings a factor 2, so cos 2x becomes −4 sin 2x.

h.en: Practice 15. A particle moves with s = 2t³ − 9t² + 12t. Find its velocity and acceleration at t = 2 s.

body.en:
v = ds/dt = 6t² − 18t + 12 and a = dv/dt = 12t − 18.

At t = 2: v = 24 − 36 + 12 = 0 m/s and a = 24 − 18 = 6 m/s².

A zero velocity means the particle is momentarily at rest, yet it still has acceleration - the turning point of its motion.

h.en: Practice 16. Find and classify the stationary points of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x.

body.en:
f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), so the stationary points are x = 1 and x = 3.

f″(x) = 6x − 12: f″(1) = −6 < 0 → maximum, f(1) = 4; f″(3) = 6 > 0 → minimum, f(3) = 0.

The curve rises to 4, falls to 0 and then climbs again.

v = ds/dt ;  a = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
f′(x) = 0 ;  f″ < 0 maximum, f″ > 0 minimum

q.en: Differentiate f(x) = x² from first principles.

a.en:
Step 1: f(x + h) − f(x) = (x + h)² − x² = 2xh + h².

Step 2: divide by h → 2x + h.

Step 3: let h → 0, so f′(x) = 2x.

At x = 1 the slope is 2 and at x = 3 it is 6 - the tangent gets steeper as x grows.

q.en: Differentiate f(x) = √x from first principles.

a.en:
Write [√(x + h) − √x]/h and multiply top and bottom by the conjugate √(x + h) + √x.

The numerator becomes (x + h) − x = h, so the expression is h / {h[√(x + h) + √x]} = 1/[√(x + h) + √x].

Let h → 0: f′(x) = 1/(√x + √x) = 1/(2√x).

q.en: Differentiate y = 3x² − 5x + 2 and find the slope at x = 2.

a.en:
Term by term: d(3x²)/dx = 6x, d(−5x)/dx = −5, d(2)/dx = 0.

So dy/dx = 6x − 5.

At x = 2 the slope is 12 − 5 = 7.

q.en: Differentiate y = x³ + 2x² − 7x + 1.

a.en:
Each term is a power of x, so differentiate term by term.

3x² + 4x − 7 + 0, that is dy/dx = 3x² + 4x − 7.

The constant 1 differentiates to 0, and −7x differentiates to −7.

q.en: Differentiate y = x²(3x + 5) using the product rule.

a.en:
Take u = x² and v = 3x + 5, so u′ = 2x and v′ = 3.

(uv)′ = u′v + uv′ = 2x(3x + 5) + x²(3) = 6x² + 10x + 3x².

So dy/dx = 9x² + 10x.

Check by expanding first: y = 3x³ + 5x², whose derivative is the same.

q.en: Differentiate y = (x + 1)(x² + 3).
Differentiate y = (2x + 1)/(x − 1) using the quotient rule.

a.en:
u = 2x + 1, v = x − 1, so u′ = 2 and v′ = 1.

(u/v)′ = [2(x − 1) − (2x + 1)(1)]/(x − 1)² = (2x − 2 − 2x − 1)/(x − 1)².

So dy/dx = −3/(x − 1)², which is negative for every x ≠ 1.

q.en: Differentiate y = x/(x² + 1).

a.en:
u = x, v = x² + 1, so u′ = 1 and v′ = 2x.

(u/v)′ = [1(x² + 1) − x(2x)]/(x² + 1)² = (x² + 1 − 2x²)/(x² + 1)².

So dy/dx = (1 − x²)/(x² + 1)².

The slope is zero at x = 1, which is where this curve has its maximum.

q.en: Differentiate y = (3x + 2)⁵.

a.en:
This is a function of a function: the outside is a fifth power and the inside is 3x + 2.

Take u = 3x + 2: dy/du = 5u⁴ and du/dx = 3.

dy/dx = 5u⁴ × 3 = 15(3x + 2)⁴.

The factor 3 is compulsory - without it the answer would only be right for (x + 2)⁵.

q.en: Differentiate y = sin 5x.

a.en:
The outside is sin and the inside is 5x, whose derivative is 5.

dy/dx = cos(5x) × 5 = 5 cos 5x.

At x = 0 the slope is 5, which is why the graph of sin 5x rises five times as fast as sin x.

q.en: Differentiate y = e^(3x).

a.en:
The derivative of e^u is e^u, so the only extra work is the inside derivative.

dy/dx = e^(3x) × 3 = 3e^(3x).

Similarly y = e^(−2x) gives −2e^(−2x): a negative inside derivative makes the function decrease.

q.en: Differentiate y = √(x² + 1).

a.en:
Write the root as a power: y = (x² + 1)^(1/2).

dy/dx = (1/2)(x² + 1)^(−1/2) × 2x = x(x² + 1)^(−1/2).

So dy/dx = x/√(x² + 1).

At x = 0 the slope is 0, which matches the flat bottom of the curve there.

q.en: Differentiate y = log(sin x).

a.en:
For y = log[f(x)] the derivative is f′(x)/f(x).

Here f(x) = sin x and f′(x) = cos x, so dy/dx = cos x/sin x.

That is dy/dx = cot x.

q.en: Find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25 and hence the slope at (3, 4).

a.en:
Differentiate every term with respect to x, remembering that y is a function of x: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0.

So dy/dx = −x/y.

At (3, 4): dy/dx = −3/4. The tangent there is y − 4 = (−3/4)(x − 3), that is 3x + 4y = 25.

q.en: Find dy/dx for x² + xy + y² = 7.

a.en:
The middle term is a product, so use the product rule on xy: derivative = y + x(dy/dx).

Differentiating the whole equation: 2x + y + x(dy/dx) + 2y(dy/dx) = 0.

Factorise: (x + 2y)(dy/dx) = −(2x + y), so dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y).

q.en: Find dy/dx for the parametric curve x = at², y = 2at.

a.en:
Differentiate each with respect to t: dx/dt = 2at and dy/dt = 2a.

dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 2a/(2at) = 1/t.

At t = 2 the slope is 1/2, and the point is (4a, 4a).

q.en: Find dy/dx for x = a cos θ, y = a sin θ.

a.en:
dx/dθ = −a sin θ and dy/dθ = a cos θ.

dy/dx = a cos θ /(−a sin θ) = −cot θ.

This matches the implicit answer for x² + y² = a², where dy/dx = −x/y = −cot θ.

q.en: Differentiate y = xˣ.

a.en:
The variable is in both the base and the power, so take logarithms: log y = x log x.

Differentiate both sides: (1/y)(dy/dx) = 1·log x + x·(1/x) = 1 + log x.

Multiply by y: dy/dx = xˣ(1 + log x).

Note that 1 + log x = 0 at x = 1/e, the minimum of the curve for x > 0.

q.en: Differentiate y = (1 + x)ˣ.

a.en:
Take logs: log y = x log(1 + x).

Differentiate: (1/y)(dy/dx) = log(1 + x) + x/(1 + x).

So dy/dx = (1 + x)ˣ[log(1 + x) + x/(1 + x)].

At x = 0 this gives 1·(0 + 0) = 0, and indeed the curve of (1 + x)ˣ is flat at x = 0.

q.en: Find the second derivative of y = x⁴.

a.en:
First derivative: y′ = 4x³.

Differentiate again: y″ = 12x².

Since y″ ≥ 0 everywhere, the curve y = x⁴ is concave up on both sides of the origin.

q.en: Find the second derivative of y = sin 3x.

a.en:
First derivative: y′ = 3 cos 3x (chain rule brings the factor 3).

Differentiate again: y″ = 3 × (−3 sin 3x) = −9 sin 3x.

Each differentiation multiplies by 3, and the function moves sin → cos → −sin.

q.en: A particle moves with s = t³ − 6t² + 8t − 4 (s in metres, t in seconds). Find the velocity and acceleration at t = 3 s.

a.en:
v = ds/dt = 3t² − 12t + 8 and a = dv/dt = 6t − 12.

At t = 3: v = 27 − 36 + 8 = −1 m/s and a = 18 − 12 = 6 m/s².

The negative velocity means the particle is moving backwards at that instant, while the positive acceleration means the velocity is increasing - it is slowing down.

q.en: Find the stationary points of f(x) = x³ − 3x + 2 and classify them.

a.en:
f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x² − 1), so f′(x) = 0 at x = 1 and x = −1.

f″(x) = 6x, so f″(−1) = −6 < 0 → maximum at x = −1, and f″(1) = 6 > 0 → minimum at x = 1.

The values are f(−1) = −1 + 3 + 2 = 4 and f(1) = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0.

q.en: Find and classify the stationary points of f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x.

a.en:
f′(x) = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2), so f′(x) = 0 at x = 1 and x = 2.

f″(x) = 12x − 18: f″(1) = −6 < 0 → maximum, value f(1) = 5; f″(2) = 6 > 0 → minimum, value f(2) = 4.

The curve rises to 5, dips to 4 and then climbs again.

q.en: What does dy/dx mean geometrically?

a.en: The slope of the tangent to the curve at that point - the rate at which y changes with x.

q.en: Define the derivative in words.

a.en: The limit of [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h as h tends to zero.

q.en: Why can h not be put equal to zero at the start?

a.en: Because the expression would become 0/0. The h in the denominator must be cancelled first, and only then is h taken to zero.

q.en: What is the derivative of a constant, and why?

a.en: Zero: a horizontal line has no change, so its slope is 0.

q.en: Can a continuous function fail to have a derivative?

a.en: Yes. At a sharp corner, such as y = |x| at x = 0, the left and right slopes differ, so no single tangent slope exists.

q.en: State the product rule.

a.en: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ - differentiate one factor at a time and add.

q.en: State the quotient rule.

a.en: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v², with the derivative of the numerator first.

q.en: Why is (uv)′ not u′v′?

a.en: Because y = x²(3x + 5) would then differentiate to 6x, while the true answer is 9x² + 10x. The rule accounts for both factors changing at once.

q.en: State the chain rule.

a.en: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx: differentiate the outside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

q.en: Differentiate sin 5x.

a.en: 5 cos 5x. The inside derivative 5 must be included.

q.en: Differentiate (3x + 2)⁵.

a.en: 15(3x + 2)⁴: 5(3x + 2)⁴ from the power and 3 from the inside.

q.en: What is an implicit function?

a.en: One where x and y are mixed in a single equation, such as x² + y² = 25, so y is not written alone.

q.en: When differentiating an implicit equation, what extra factor appears?

a.en: dy/dx. Every y-term gains one, because y is a function of x (chain rule).

q.en: How do you find dy/dx for a parametric curve?

a.en: Differentiate both x and y with respect to the parameter, then divide: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

q.en: When do you use logarithmic differentiation?

a.en: When the variable appears in the power (xˣ), or when the expression is a long product or quotient.

q.en: What do velocity and acceleration mean in calculus?

a.en: v = ds/dt (rate of change of position) and a = dv/dt = d²s/dt² (rate of change of velocity).

q.en: How do you test whether a stationary point is a maximum or a minimum?

a.en: Use the second derivative: f″ < 0 gives a maximum, f″ > 0 a minimum. If f″ = 0, check the sign of f′ on both sides.
